mappings.conceptual_understanding: Rational numbers can be represented in many equivalent ways
Rational numbers can be approximated to support judgements of magnitude and reasonableness
Numbers with repeated factors can be expressed using exponential notation
The inverse relationships between addition and subtraction and multiplication and division can be used to add, subtract, multiply or divide rational numbers
Multiplying a positive number by a number greater than 0 and less than 1 results in a smaller number
Dividing a positive number by a number greater than 0 and less than 1 results in a larger number
Fractions, percentages, ratios and rates are different ways of representing a proportional relationship between quantities
Mathematical modelling can be used to represent and analyse financial and other real-world situations and support informed decision-making
Patterns and relationships between variables can be described algebraically and graphed to solve problems and support inferences
Algebraic expressions can be represented in infinitely many different but equivalent ways
The commutative and associative properties apply to addition and multiplication, but not to subtraction and division
The distributive property of multiplication over addition and subtraction can be used to support efficient calculation
Parallel and intersecting lines have properties that can be used to deduce relationships between the angles formed
Measurable attributes of 2-dimensional shapes and 3-dimensional objects can be determined based on the known properties of the shape or solid
In any circle, the ratio of the circumference to the diameter is always the same and is represented by the number pi (π)
Objects can be represented in two-dimensions in different ways
Shapes can be classified and compared by their geometrical properties
Geometrical transformations of points and 2-dimensional shapes can be represented on a Cartesian plane
Data can be organised and represented in different ways to inform, justify and persuade conclusions
Variation in data can be measured and used to describe and compare data sets
Outcomes of events can be described and their likelihood can be measured
Theoretical probabilities can predict relative frequencies of experimental data
Rational and irrational numbers can be expressed and represented in different forms depending on context and purpose
Exponential laws describe patterns in operations involving exponential notation enabling efficient calculations
Mathematical modelling can be used to represent and solve practical problems, including in financial contexts, using rational numbers and percentages
Equivalent algebraic expressions and solutions to equations can be determined by applying properties of mathematical operations and numbers
Linear relations between two variables can be represented algebraically and graphically, leading to generalised patterns and conjectures

Attributes such as length, area, volume, rates and angles of 1-, 2- and 3-dimensional objects including irregular and composite shapes can be quantified with appropriate units and used to solve problems in a range of contexts
Duration can be quantified using units of time, including 12- and 24-hour time, and compared across different time zones
Congruency and similarity can be established and used for triangles and other shapes to describe position, location and properties
Comparison of the measure of sides and angles between 2 triangles can establish a relationship of congruence or similarity from which unknown measures can be deduced
Relationships and properties of congruent and similar triangles can be used to deduce the properties of quadrilaterals
Position and location of objects in 3 dimensions can be represented using a coordinate system
Valid inferences about populations can be made by drawing conclusions from representative samples
A representative sample depends on the nature of the population and the question being considered
Complementary events in an experiment are mutually exclusive and together cover all possible outcomes
The sample space for 2 events can be presented diagrammatically in a variety of ways to determine the probabilities of specific outcomes, including compound events
Rational and irrational numbers can be represented in many forms, including on a number line, and can be used to find exact and approximate values
The parameters of quadratics and other functions determine the features of the related graph and can be adjusted depending on the purpose, context and application
Expressions involving exponent notation with integer or variable bases can be simplified or represented differently using the law of exponents
On a Cartesian plane, the coordinates of 2 distinct points can be used to determine a range of measures of their orientation in relation to each other
Mathematical modelling can be used to represent and solve problems involving changes, including financial contexts
Spatial relationships in 1, 2 and 3 dimensions can be quantified using appropriate units to solve problems in various contexts
Calculations are affected by sources of error and should be interpreted in the context of the problem
Mathematical modelling can be used to represent and solve problems involving proportion, rates, ratios and scale, including in financial contexts
Trigonometric ratios are an application of the property of similarity for right-angled triangles
Sampling methods can affect and bias the results of data collection
Different representations of data distributions can be used to compare features such as centre, shape and spread
Statistical reports provide data and analysis to support conclusions and acknowledge the strength of the evidence
Theoretical probabilities are based on the characteristics of an experiment and can be used to predict relative frequencies of experimental data
The likelihood of an event occurring can be affected by another event that has already taken place
The probability of compound events is related to the probability of the associated simple events and can be calculated in the context of the experiment
Using approximations rather than exact values affects the accuracy of results in both single and multiple calculations
Relationships between variables can be described and modelled by linear, quadratic and exponential functions applied in many contexts including financial ones
Attributes of 1-, 2- and 3-dimensional objects are described and measured in appropriate standardised units
Measurement errors impact the accuracy of results
Situations involving angles, distance and direction can be quantified using geometric properties and theorems
Data can be represented in different ways to establish relationships, while considering accuracy and bias
Claims and inferences based on data should acknowledge ethical considerations and potential sources of bias
Conditional probability can be described and interpreted for multiple events and applied in real-life contexts
The likelihood of an event occurring can be affected by another event that has already taken place
